# Aryne Generation from Aryl Halides via Photothermal Red-Light Activation

**Authors:** Cristina Preston-Herrera; Rory C. Devin; Megan E. Matter; Erin E. Stache

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, United States

## Abstract

Multistep synthetic methods requiring harsh conditions and poor atom economy are central to the generation of aryne precursors. The Kobayashi method remains the standard for aryne generation, and newer methods have relied on similar strategies of activated precursors for mild aryne generation. Here, we show the generation of arynes from commercially available aryl or heteroaryl halides via photothermal conversion under air using red light. With photothermal conversion, the high-energy aryne intermediate is formed via inhomogeneous thermal gradients. Nitrogen nucleophiles then readily trap the aryne intermediate to forge C–N bonds, an essential bond in pharmaceutical and agrochemical synthesis, simplifying traditional methods that use aryl halides as aryne precursors. A wide range of readily available heteroaryl and aryl halides undergo amination in less than 20 minutes under red light irradiation of carbon black. The product regioselectivity matches the expected distribution from aryne trapping, further supporting an aryne mechanism. Additionally, we show aryne trapping via a [4+2] cycloaddition, with a sulfur nucleophile, and a 1-pot double amination with 1,2-dibromobenzene. This photothermal method using commercially available aryl/heteroaryl halides enables on demand access to arynes without inert conditions, solvent, or additional synthetic steps, overcoming operational barriers of existing approaches.

## Abstract

Aryne intermediates have captivated synthetic chemists since their proposal in 1902 and later validation by Roberts et al. in 1953.1,2 Since then, arynes have emerged as powerful and versatile intermediates capable of engaging in a range of transformations, including cycloadditions, nucleophilic additions, and insertion reactions, to name a few (Scheme 1A).3–6 The highly reactive electrophilic intermediate has been applied in complex molecule synthesis, enabling rapid construction of densely functionalized aromatic scaffolds, heterocycles, polycyclic frameworks, total synthesis of natural products, and late-stage diversification of pharmaceutically relevant molecules.3,7–10 However, despite their broad synthetic appeal, the mild generation of arynes has relied on multistep synthesis of specialized precursors.

Deprotonation-elimination has been used as a strategy to generate arynes from activated precursors under mild conditions (Scheme 1B). For example, iodonium or thianthrenium salt precursors can generate arynes under mildly basic conditions and ambient temperatures.11–23 Similarly, halonium and oxonium precursors have emerged as effective methods for generating arynes using carbonate or phosphate bases, enabling the inclusion of electrophilic or base-sensitive functional groups.24–27 Recently, the Roberts group reported a strategy for visible light activated aryne generation from a carboxylic acid-derived precursor.28,29 However, these advancements in making arynes more accessible still require preactivation via synthetic manipulations of commercial starting materials. Aryl boronic acids have emerged as viable aryne precursors, eliminating the need for further synthesis to generate aryne intermediates.30,31 However, these precursors suffer from limited commercial availability.32 In contrast, widely available aryl halides/pseudohalides have been known as aryne precursors but require inert/dry conditions and very strong bases to overcome the high kinetic barrier for dehalogenative elimination.2,33–42

The most widely adopted synthetic approach for generating arynes is the Kobayashi method, which has played a central role in popularizing aryne chemistry over the past few decades (Scheme 1C).43,44 The mild conditions of the final elimination step belie the synthetic burden required to obtain the precursor. The preparation of o-silylaryl triflates is multistep, substrate-specific, and typically begins from aryl alcohols—limiting the scope to systems compatible with electrophilic triflation and silylation chemistry. Moreover, the use of moisture-sensitive, hazardous reagents and the need for intermediate purification complicate this approach.45–47 These practical drawbacks can become a significant barrier when evaluating diverse substrate scope or broadly applying aryne chemistry in synthesis.

Building on decades of base-promoted aryne chemistry from aryl halides, we now demonstrate how photothermal activation can simplify this transformation and broaden its accessibility. Here, we present a photothermal strategy that enables aryne generation from commercially available aryl and heteroaryl halides and potassium tert-butoxide (KOt-Bu) under red light irradiation, without solvent, precise temperature control, or additional synthesis of the precursor (Scheme 1D). This approach harnesses carbon black (CB) as an inexpensive, broadly absorbing photothermal agent (PTA) that converts light into localized heat, eliminating the need for bulk heating and enabling energetically demanding transformations under red light.48–52 By applying this method, we demonstrate the successful dehalogenative elimination of aryl and heteroaryl halides varying in electronic and steric profiles. The resulting arynes engage efficiently in amination reactions with diverse nitrogen nucleophiles, including many of the most common heterocycles found in pharmaceuticals.53 Their reactivity is further demonstrated by [4+2] cycloaddition, addition with a thiol nucleophile, and a one-pot multifunctionalization. Here, a new level of accessibility for aryne chemistry is presented using traditional base-promoted aryl halide elimination, simplifying workflows and lowering barriers to entry for synthetic chemists.

To evaluate the operational simplicity of our photothermal aryne method, reactions were conducted under air, without rea-gent purification, solvent, or stirring. Our optimized conditions included KOt-Bu as the base, CB as the photothermal agent, and irradiation for 20 minutes using a 660 nm LED chip. The arylation of 4-bromoanisole (A) with piperidine (1) was used as the model reaction (Figure 1A). We observed 64% yield with a 1:1 ratio of regioisomers (1A, 1A’) (Figure 1B entry 1). Reaction progress showed that this product distribution remained consistent throughout the reaction without product degradation (Figure 1C).

To probe the effect of halide identity on aryne formation, we evaluated other anisole derivatives. Using 4-iodoanisole gave high conversion but a lower yield due to decomposition of the aryl iodide and rapid aryne formation, leading to nonproductive side reactions (Figure 1B, entry 2).54–58 4-Chloroanisole afforded lower conversion and yield, likely due to its poorer leaving group ability (Figure 1B, entry 3).59 This observation held with 4-fluoroanisole, which proved unable to form the desired aminated product (Figure 1B, entry 4).

Control experiments further confirmed the essential role of photothermal conversion in promoting the reaction. In the absence of CB, no product formation was observed, ruling out background heating or photochemical excitation by red light alone (Figure 1B, entry 5). Omission of the base completely shut down reactivity (Figure 1B, entry 6). Changing the cation on the base from potassium to sodium led to a significant decrease in yield, likely due to stronger ion pairing that reduces the basicity under solvent-free conditions (Figure 1B, entry 7).60,61 Introducing a small volume of DMSO to aid in ion pair with potassium dissociation and base solubility resulted in an increased yield of 80% with KOt-Bu (Figure 1B, entry 8).

To validate that localized heating from CB is the driving force, we performed the same reaction using bulk thermal heating at 100 °C in an oil bath. The specific temperature was chosen based on the maximum reaction temperature observed during thermocouple measurements (Figure S4). Despite the elevated temperature, only 11% yield was obtained (Figure 1B entry 9). Longer reaction times led to 22% after 24 h, in agreement with prior literature reporting long reaction times for similar transformations even at 135 °C.62,63 Replacing the light source with a commercially available 660 nm Kessil resulted in slightly lower yields (Figure 1B entry. 10), likely due to the lower intensity of the light source (6.5 W vs. 4 W).

Lastly, to demonstrate that this method follows the typical aryne distortion model, we switched 4-bromoanisole to 2- or 3-bromoanisole. Here, the more linear (distorted) aryne carbon is the preferred site of nucleophilic attack, yielding a single regioisomer.64 Consistent with this prediction, the resultant aryne under standard photothermal conditions exclusively gave the meta piperidine adduct in 70–72% yield. (Figure 1D).

A broad array of aryl halides, including those bearing electronically diverse and sterically encumbered substituents, were successfully arylated under the optimized photothermal conditions, demonstrating the generality of this method. Aryl halides with electron-withdrawing substituents, such as 4-bromotrifluoromethylbenzene, afforded an isolated yield of 78% (Figure 2, 1C, 1C’).

Notably, 4-fluoroaryl bromide favored aryne formation, where deprotonation, elimination of bromide, and piperidine addition outpaced competing SNAr, delivering the aryne product in 76% yield with <10% of the brominated SNAr byproduct (Figure 2, 1D, 1D’). Electron-rich and electron-neutral aryl halides also performed well, with dimethylamino-substituted reaching 56% yield (Figure 2, 1G,1 G’) and tert-butyl benzyne achieving 51% yield (Figure 2, 1I, 1I’). These results highlight the robustness of this system, which operates effectively across a range of electronic environments—an advantage over many traditional C–N coupling methods that are highly sensitive to substrate electronics.65,66

Excitingly, readily available, multisubstituted aryl halides performed well under the photothermal benzyne conditions. Notably, 1-bromo-2-fluoro-4-methylbenzene resulted in 79% yield for the addition of piperidine to yield 1L and 1L’ in a 1.5 to 1.0 ratio (Figure 2, 1L, 1L’). This reactivity showcases how applicable the photothermal system can be leveraged when synthesizing molecules with pharmaceutically relevant motifs such as fluoro groups (Figure 2, 1C, 1C’, 1D, 1D’, 1L, 1L’) and oxazolines (Figure 2, 1J).67,68

Further expanding the scope, 5-bromopyridine derivatives bearing substituents at the 2-position also showed good functional group tolerance. Substrates with electron-withdrawing groups such as trifluoromethyl gave 66% yield (Figure 2, 1P, 1P’), while methyl and dimethylamino substituents afforded 49% (Figure 2, 1R, 1R’) and 60% (Figure 2, 1S, 1S’) yields, respectively. However, a lower yield of 33% was observed with 3-bromoquinoline (Figure 2, 1T, 1T’), likely due to competing protodehalogenation leading to quinoline formation. Lastly, heteroaromatic electrophiles yielded a mixture of three products, likely due to the unselective nature of deprotonation. Addition to the 5 position gave the major regioisomer, and addition to the 6 position afforded the minor product for each substrate, respectively (Figure 2, 1U-1U”, 1V-1V”, 1W-1W”).

Next, we examined the capabilities of our system for the arylation of various nitrogen nucleophiles. While both chloro- and bromobenzene performed similarly well in the system, we opted to use the less expensive and ubiquitous chlorobenzene to evaluate the nucleophile scope. Each nucleophile formed only one product following the attack on the equivalent electrophilic positions of the benzyne intermediate. Reflecting the high electrophilicity of benzyne, a wide range of nucleophiles could be N-arylated. Primary and secondary alkylamines reacted to produce the corresponding anilines in acceptable to moderate yields (Figure 3, 1–8X). However, slower reactivity brought on by increased steric hindrance resulted in lower yields due to competition with tert-butoxide as a nucleophile (9–11X). Less nucleophilic anilines were also relatively well tolerated, and some conversion was even observed for highly hindered anilines (12–13X). Further, diarylamines and heterocycles such as indole and benzimidazole were arylated despite their poor nucleophilicity (14–16X). For substrate 14, with a relatively acidic N-H bond, isolation of the potassium salt after treatment with potassium tert-butoxide or sodium bis(trimethylsilyl)amide (NaHMDS) significantly increased the yield from 47 to 82% of the desired products (14X, Figure S56).

To highlight the versatility of this photothermal platform, we extended it beyond amination to other canonical aryne reactions. Aryne trapping with 2,4-dimethylbenzenethiol, recently reported as the first step in the synthesis of the antidepressant Trintellix, proceeded in 77% yield (Figure 4A, 17Y).69 Tetraphenylcyclopentadienone, a benchmark aryne trap employed in Kobayashi and iodonium precursor systems, delivered the [4+2] cycloadduct in 38% yield (Figure 4A, 18Y).3,70,71 Double amination of 1,2-dibromobenzene furnished the 1,3-diaminobenzene in 56% yield under conditions that bypass the stringent dryness, elevated temperatures, and >36 h reaction time of a prior protocol (Figure 4B, 1Z).62 This further showcases the ease of aryne trapping and reaction screening for industrially relevant motifs.72 Finally, the operational simplicity of this strategy is highlighted by a gram-scale synthesis using 4-bromoanisole. Upon extending the irradiation time to 1 h, the desired product was obtained in 66% yield, matching the yield from the smaller-scale reaction (Figure 4C).

## CONCLUSIONS

Here, we present a simple strategy for aryne generation from abundant aryl halides without multistep precursor synthesis or exclusion of ambient air and water. By harnessing photothermal conversion using inexpensive carbon black and red-light irradiation, our protocol rapidly unlocks aryne intermediates compatible with many different functional groups. The combination of a practical, scalable, and accessible entry point to aryne chemistry enables a new pathway to leverage these reactive intermediates across a wide range of applications in chemical synthesis.
